prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After reading all eight round-1 statements I keep a single-part prize for B039, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. The reason is the discovery-first test I try to apply: Kane and Mele introduced a new organising principle, a Z2 invariant that forces protected edge states, and Molenkamp's group then went to nature and found quantised edge conduction in HgTe wells. That is a clue from nature, not elegant theory alone. The concept has been confirmed independently for about fifteen to twenty years, and has spread to 3D materials, photonic and cold-atom systems. The 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions and phases, not time-reversal-protected Z2 physics, so I do not see a real overlap. The prediction-then-observation structure also gives the committee a three-name credit that can be explained in one sentence. On the chair's question: confined to the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators with the HgTe realisation, the citation is defensible to external reviewers, provided the Secretary's expert requests confirm the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang chronology before the vote.
statement.case_against: The credit is the weak point and I do not want to hide it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the host, and without that the Molenkamp experiment would not have been a decisive test. Zhang has died, so he cannot be honoured, but Bernevig and Hughes remain outside the three-name limit. Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy, Hasan and Cava made the 3D case. If the committee decides that the 2D effect and 3D topological insulators are two achievements, then no three-person set fits both fairly, and a two-part prize would exceed the limit of three people. The citation must therefore be worded around the 2D effect and the HgTe test and must not claim the whole field. A residual risk is that external experts rate the BHZ contribution as decisive, in which case I would reconsider and move to B022, whose credit is cleaner.

responses.point: Olsson keeps the optical lattice clock first, calls it an invention that is also a discovery, and answers my sixth-place ranking by saying the pending redefinition of the second is a consequence of the result, not a condition for it.
responses.response: I accept her point on the redefinition and withdraw it as an objection: the 10^-18 agreement between independent clocks stands by itself and the committee should not wait for a metrology decision. The chair's question about what new fact about nature the clock has already delivered is mine, and Olsson and Lindroth have given an honest answer, namely millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, limits on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings, and many-body physics inside the clock. That moves me, since it is more than a smaller error bar. I still rank B039 above it. The magic-wavelength lattice is a brilliant instrument, but the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-ion prize already recognised the toolbox of precision spectroscopy, whereas band topology is a new idea about what matter can do. This is a judgement about novelty and I accept it is not decisive; B022 stays my first alternative.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is a measurement technique that changes what can be observed, with clean two-name attribution and independent confirmation at JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and Tokyo.
responses.response: The attribution is cleaner than for any other candidate, and I grant that willingly. Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's accuracy record are both real, and I would defer to Kroll on whether both names are essential. My residual concern is the precedent of a further precision-timekeeping prize after 2005 and 2012, so the citation would have to name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly. If the committee prefers a citation on those terms I could vote for it, but I do not think clean credit should outweigh conceptual weight when the credit for B039, though more contested, is still defensible within the supplied names. I also note that Kroll and I agree that B028 should not be put forward with leadership-based credit.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first on the strength of the theory-experiment loop and long independent confirmation, and he flags the Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and 3D omissions and his reliance on memory for the priority history.
responses.response: We agree on the core, and we both want the citation kept to the 2D case. Eriksson and Mehlig use wording on topological insulators in general, and I think that is a mistake: it invites the objection that we have ignored Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan and Cava. My wording on the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators with HgTe realisation is narrower and says what the trio did. Since both of us are working from memory on priority, I would ask that the Secretary's expert requests cover Bernevig, Hughes and Hasan before the vote, and I accept that this is partly my own task.

responses.point: Johansson has moved topological insulators to the top of her list, sees no real overlap with the 2016 prize, and values the breadth of support from members with different backgrounds.
responses.response: I agree on the overlap and have softened my own round-1 worry. Time-reversal-protected Z2 physics, with edge states that survive disorder, is a different thing from the phase-transition work of 2016. I would add a caution to her argument from breadth: seven of eight rankings is useful information, but it is not a substitute for judging the credit. I am not relying on it, and I hope nobody else is. Her wording and mine are almost identical, and I think we can settle on that citation.

uncertainties: Whether the external experts regard the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal as so decisive that the trio Kane, Mele, Molenkamp cannot be defended.
Whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and 3D topological insulators are one achievement or two; if two, the three-person limit forces a choice I cannot make fairly.
How much weight to give novelty over metrological impact and clean credit, which is the real dividing line between B039 and B022 and is a matter of taste as much as evidence.
I am working from memory on the priority chronology and outside my own field, and defer to the condensed-matter and AMO members on details.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name arises from my profile. My supervisor David Gross, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string group are not connected to any shortlisted ballot. Topological insulators and optical clocks are outside my own field. As Secretary I will carry out the external-expert requests, which is a procedural duty and not a conflict. No recusal is needed, and I note the chair's recorded flags for Johansson, Pearce, Kroll and Lindroth.
